summary: Zuicho Tachibana (1890–1968) worked in history, archaeology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Buddhist studies. He studied under Kōzui Ōtani around 1903 and under Edward Denison Ross circa 1910–1912.

Zuiei Ito (1942–2020) specialized in Buddhist studies and Indology, earning degrees at Waseda University and the University of Tokyo. He served as professor of Buddhist studies at Rissho University (1980–2013) and lectured at Tokyo, Waseda, and Shinshu Universities.

Zuigan Goto (1879–1965) was a Buddhist studies figure who studied at the Second Higher School, the University of Tokyo (1903–1906), and under Sōkatsu Shaku (circa 1906–1914). He served as president of Hanazono University in 1932.

Zuiho Yamaguchi (1926–2023) was a Tibetologist and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo and under Jacques Bacot and Rolf A. Stein in France. He held posts at CNRS, Toyo Bunko, Tokyo University (1970–1986), and Nagoya University.

Zuiryu Nakamura (1915–1995) worked in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He studied under Susumu Yamaguchi in 1944 and became a professor in the Department of Buddhist Studies at Rissho University in 1945.
Gyurme tubten nyinje studied under Shechen Gyaltsab and Jamyang Khyentse Chökyi Lodrö.
Pad+ma la studied under Dilgo Khyentse and Dudjom Rinpoche.

Édouard Chavannes (1865–1918) was a scholar of sinology, history, archaeology, and Buddhist studies. He studied at the École Normale Supérieure, INALCO, and Collège de France, where he later served as professor from 1893 to 1918.

Édouard Huber (1879–1914) worked in sinology, Buddhist studies, and linguistics. He studied in Paris under Sylvain Lévi and Johann Baptist Schibenegg, and held teaching posts at the École Française d'Extrême-Orient from 1901 until 1914.

Émile Benveniste (1902–1976) specialized in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. After studying under Antoine Meillet and Sylvain Lévi, he taught at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (1927–1969) and held the comparative grammar chair at Collège de France (1937–1969).
Émile Chartier (1868–1951) was a philosopher who studied at Lycée Pierre-Corneille (~1881–1886) and École Normale Supérieure (~1889–1892).

Émile Chatelain (1851–1933) worked in linguistics, history, and archaeology. He studied at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1872–1876), later holding a post there (~1881–1933) after serving at the École française de Rome (1876–1877).

Émile Durkheim (1858–1917) was a scholar of religious studies and sociology who studied at the École Normale Supérieure and under Wilhelm Wundt. He held posts at the University of Bordeaux (1887–1902) and Sorbonne University (~1902–1917).

Émile Senart (1847–1928) worked in Indology, Buddhist studies, and archaeology. He studied at the universities of Munich and Göttingen, the latter under Theodor Benfey, and served as professor at the Collège de France and president of the Société Asiatique (1908–1928).

Émile-Louis Burnouf (1821–1907) specialized in Indology and linguistics. He studied under Jean-Louis and Eugène Burnouf, attended the École Normale Supérieure and University of Paris, and served as professor at Nancy (1854–1867) and director of the École française d'Athènes (1867–1875).
Étienne Balázs (1905–1963) was a historian and sinologist who studied under Otto Franke from 1923 to 1930. He held posts at the CNRS (from 1949) and the University of Paris (~1949–1963).

Étienne Lamotte (1903–1983) was a Buddhist studies and Indology scholar. He studied under Louis de La Vallée Poussin, Sylvain Lévi, and others, and served as professor at KU Leuven (1932–1974) and president at UCLouvain (1950–1959).

Ñāṇavīra Thera (1920–1965) was a Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar who studied at Magdalene College and under Pelene Siri Vajirañāṇa (~1949–1950). He also served in the Royal Artillery (1939–1941) and the Intelligence Corps (1941–1945).

Ösel Tendzin (1943–1990) was a Buddhist studies figure who studied at Fordham University and under Swami Satchidananda Saraswati and Chögyam Trungpa. He was executive vice president of Vajradhatu in 1973 and succeeded Trungpa in 1987.
Ülo Valk (born 1962) specializes in religious studies and Indology. He studied at and joined the faculty of the University of Tartu (~1995), and served as editor of Numen (~2007–2013).
